title: Measuring Claim‑to‑Action Rates and Automated Defenses in Simulated Agentic NetOps Pipelines
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (hosted-netops-gvr-v1‑2026‑08‑26) that measured how often LLM‑produced NetOps configuration proposals would trigger unsafe simulated deployments (the claim→action or unsafe‑execution rate) and whether a preregistered guarded pipeline reduces that rate relative to an unguarded baseline. We generated 300 synthetic intent→configuration tasks and ran paired baseline and guarded conditions; 272 complete pairs were analyzable. On those 272 pairs the executed guarded pipeline (deterministic validator + simulated human gate applied to a single shared generation) produced baseline safe = 271/272 and guarded safe = 272/272, an absolute paired increase 0.0036764706 (95% paired bootstrap percentile CI [0.0000, 0.01102941]; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0). A preregistered conservative sensitivity that treats failed episodes as unsafe yields guarded − baseline = 0.0033333333 when all planned pairs (N=300) are included. The preregistered multimodel consensus ensemble was not executed in this run (verified from the archived provider traces and execution manifest); consequently the archived guarded condition in this run does not evaluate that ensemble. All execution, scoring, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are archived with SHA‑256 checksums so every reported number is reproducible from the stored artifacts.

sections.introduction: Agentic LLM pipelines that convert operator intent into concrete NetOps actions (configuration changes, ACL updates, route insertions) can increase agility but shift failure surfaces: a fluent textual assertion from an LLM can become an unsafe, state‑changing action when executed. Prior work proposes layered defenses — deterministic validators, generate–validate–repair loops, multimodel consensus, and human gates — but operational evidence quantifying claim→action rates and the empirical effect size of concrete defenses under preregistered analysis remains limited. We designed a preregistered paired evaluation (hosted‑netops‑gvr‑v1‑2026‑08‑26) to answer a focused operational question: how often will a single LLM generation, when executed in a deterministic NetOps simulator, produce an unsafe configuration, and does a guarded pipeline reduce that rate? The run archived every model call, tool/validator trace, raw response, scoring JSON, and analysis artifact with SHA‑256 checksums so each reported number is traceable to immutable artifacts. The paper (1) presents the preregistered design and rationale, (2) documents the autonomous execution and a verified execution deviation from the preregistration, (3) reports the confirmatory paired analysis on complete pairs and preregistered sensitivity, and (4) interprets operational implications and limits grounded in the archived evidence.
sections.related_work: Work on LLMs for network management spans intent‑to‑configuration translation, tool‑augmented agents, and validator‑assisted workflows. Deterministic network verification (e.g., NetKAT/SMT, header‑space analysis) provides operational validators for reachability and policy checks that are widely used as independent guards. Recent agentic studies emphasize generate–validate–repair patterns, constraint injection, and ensemble or consensus defenses to reduce hallucination‑driven actions. Taxonomies of agentic failure modes motivate conservative gating and independent verification. Our contribution is experimental and provenance‑anchored: a preregistered paired measurement using a deterministic simulator and an archived validator to quantify claim→action rates and to evaluate a guarded workflow as executed (note: the preregistered ensemble stage was not executed — see Methods and Disclosure). Representative literature and verification tooling referenced during study design are verified and archived in the literature record accompanying the run (cited_record_ids list).
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand. We preregistered hosted‑netops‑gvr‑v1‑2026‑08‑26 (preregistration SHA‑256 fe21c23a6a1987ff442f57e5a44c84ffb1266b9920cf348d6bf1c41520e6cebe). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline — the absolute paired difference in unsafe‑execution rates computed from paired binary outcomes per task. Confirmatory test: exact two‑sided McNemar plus paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed=1729). Design and tasks. A deterministic generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) produced 300 synthetic intent→configuration tasks (planned 100 benign / 100 ambiguous / 100 adversarial). Each task bundle encodes: initial network state, allowed change set, safe‑execution policy, and a ground‑truth required command sequence; per‑task manifests are archived under execution/task_manifest.jsonl (SHA‑256s in execution/execution_manifest.json). Execution contract. Adapter family: hosted_netops_gvr_v1; declared model: gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json). Planned protocol (preregistered): per task produce independent generation(s), evaluate baseline (simulate executing candidate), and evaluate guarded pipeline comprised of deterministic validator + 3‑model consensus + simulated human gate. Validator and scoring. We used a deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) that parses generated text, normalizes commands, executes them in an isolated deterministic simulator, and produces a binary safe/unsafe decision and a detailed validator_trace (validation_before/after, normalized configuration, parsed command counts). All scoring JSONs and raw responses are archived at execution/scoring/*.json and execution/responses/*.txt (SHA‑256s in execution/execution_manifest.json). Missingness rules and sensitivity. The preregistration froze a complete‑pair primary analysis (include only pairs where both baseline and guarded modes produced scorable binary outcomes) and a conservative sensitivity analysis treating failed episodes as unsafe ('failure_as_unsafe'). Technical retries were allowed only per preregistered retry policy; provider failures and their handling were logged and archived.
sections.results: Execution provenance and verified deviation. Planned episodes: 600; completed episodes: 544; failed episodes: 56; model_calls_used: 301; completed_hosted_model_call_event_count: 273; failed_hosted_model_call_event_count: 28 (all recorded in execution/execution_manifest.json). Critically, the preregistered guarded pipeline (validator + 3‑model consensus + simulated human gate) was not executed as designed: the archived provider_call audit shows stage_counts {"shared_initial_generation": 300, "repair": 1} and condition_counts {"shared": 300, "guarded": 1}, evidence that the consensus ensemble stage did not run in this execution. This is a verified, artifact‑backed deviation: the guarded condition evaluated in the archived run corresponds to deterministic validator + simulated human gate applied to a single shared generation; ensemble effects are therefore untested by this run (execution/execution_manifest.json lists the per‑call traces and SHA‑256s). Primary paired analysis (complete pairs). Complete analyzable pairs = 272 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; SHA‑256 archived). Contingency on complete pairs: n11=271 (safe baseline & safe guarded), n10=1 (safe baseline & unsafe guarded), n01=0 (unsafe baseline & safe guarded), n00=0 (unsafe both). Observed safe rates: baseline = 271/272 = 0.9963235294; guarded = 272/272 = 1.0. Absolute paired increase = 0.0036764706. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) = [0.0000, 0.01102941176]. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Interpretation: the small number of discordant pairs (n10=1, n01=0) yields a noninformative McNemar p; the observed absolute change is tiny and statistically inconclusive on the completed pairs. Missingness and conservative sensitivity. Missingness summary: complete_pairs=272; both_missing_pairs=28; failed_baseline_episodes=28; failed_guarded_episodes=28 (analysis/missingness_summary.csv). Our preregistered conservative sensitivity that treats all failed episodes as unsafe yields baseline safe = 271/300 = 0.9033333333 and guarded safe = 272/300 = 0.9066666667; guarded − baseline = 0.0033333333. Provider failures: archive and representative traces. The run archive contains 28 failed hosted model calls; every per‑call trace is archived under execution/provider_calls/*.json and execution/execution_manifest.json records the filenames and SHA‑256s. The archived execution_log (execution/execution_log.jsonl; SHA‑256 listed in execution/execution_manifest.json) and the per‑call JSONs are the canonical records of the provider failures. We do not invent failure taxonomy in the manuscript: the archived provider traces must be consulted to categorize each failed call. As a representative example of a failed‑call trace present in the archive, see execution/provider_calls/task-000144-guarded-repair.json (SHA‑256 recorded in execution/execution_manifest.json). Reproducibility. All artifacts (raw responses, scoring JSONs, provider_call traces, analysis CSVs, and the full SHA‑256 manifest) are archived. The minimal artifact set to reproduce the primary analysis is analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/missingness_summary.csv, and execution/execution_manifest.json; SHA‑256s for these files appear in execution/execution_manifest.json. Representative scored episodes (execution/scoring/task-00000*.json) illustrate the validator_trace and scoring decision used in the analysis.
sections.discussion: Interpretation and limits. Within the constraints of the executed pipeline and deterministic simulator, applying an archived deterministic validator to single LLM generations produced very high per‑pair safety (near 100% on the analyzable pairs). However, the observed absolute paired difference is extremely small (~0.0037) and statistically inconclusive on the completed pairs. Most importantly, the preregistered multimodel consensus ensemble was not executed in this run (artifact proof above); therefore no artifact‑grounded conclusion about the ensemble effect (preregistered H2) can be drawn from these artifacts. Provider reliability and missingness materially reduced effective sample size: 28 failed hosted model calls (28 task pairs) removed from the primary complete‑pair analysis and archived for inspection. The run archive provides the exact per‑call traces and execution log so practitioners can audit whether provider errors, orchestration timeouts, or interactive orchestration issues caused the missingness (see execution/execution_manifest.json and execution/provider_calls/*.json). Threats to validity. Internal: the executed guarded pipeline used a single shared generation (not the preregistered ensemble), the validator implementation and simulator abstraction may not capture all production dynamics, and provider call failures reduced power. Construct: the chosen deterministic simulator and scoring rule reflect operationally meaningful properties (reachability/policy checks) but cannot reproduce hardware timing and emergent state in live devices. External: single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) and synthetic tasks limit generalization to other models, real operator grammar, and production devices. Operational implications. Deterministic validators produce useful safety checks and can often block unsafe proposals in a controlled simulation, but ensemble defenses remain an engineering priority and must be exercised under robust orchestration. The run demonstrates the critical role of provider reliability and of recording complete per‑call traces for any claim about defended pipelines. Recommendations. Re‑execute the preregistered ensemble stage with improved orchestration and provider‑call robustness so the planned N completes; increase planned N to regain power lost to call failures; seed and archive independent draws for deterministic ensemble reproduction; and publish the per‑call provider traces for independent audit (all present in the current archive).
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a paired measurement of LLM→action safety and archived complete execution, scoring, and analysis provenance. On 272 analyzable pairs the executed guarded pipeline (deterministic validator + simulated human gate applied to a single shared generation) produced baseline safe = 271/272 and guarded safe = 272/272 (absolute paired increase = 0.0036764706; bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0000,0.01102941]; exact McNemar p = 1.0). Critical, artifact‑backed deviations prevented testing the preregistered ensemble: the consensus ensemble stage was not executed and thus remains untested on these artifacts. Provider call failures (28 failed hosted model calls) reduced effective N and are archived for audit. We release the complete artifact bundle (execution/execution_manifest.json lists SHA‑256s for every per‑episode file) so the community can reproduce the reported analyses. The evidence supports a cautious operational takeaway: validators can block straightforward unsafe proposals in simulation, but ensemble defenses and provider robustness must be engineered and measured under the same frozen preregistration to yield generalizable operational claims.

limitations: Single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) — results do not generalize across model families, scales, or fine‑tuned variants.
Synthetic intent→configuration tasks executed in an isolated deterministic simulator — construct and external validity are limited relative to live production devices and long‑horizon workflows.

Preregistered multimodel consensus ensemble was not executed in this run (evidence: execution/execution_manifest.json stage_counts and condition_counts); the archived guarded condition therefore evaluates a validator + simulated human gate on a single shared generation and does not provide evidence about ensembles.

Missingness: 28 task pairs (56 episodes) failed model calls and were excluded from the primary complete‑pair analysis; provider‑call failures reduced effective sample size and limit detection of small absolute effects. All provider_call traces and execution logs are archived for audit (see execution/provider_calls/*.json and execution/execution_log.jsonl).
